headline_findings: This comparison covers two papers - one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper - and does not describe either condition in general.

The Lyme disease paper provides detailed dollar cost figures by disease stage, while the Long COVID paper reports no cost, income-loss, or insurance data at all, so no direct dollar-for-dollar comparison between the two conditions is possible.

Both papers show that the way cases are identified or defined (clinical diagnosis criteria for Lyme disease, ICD-10 code versus algorithm for Long COVID) changes how undercounted or demographically skewed the condition appears in official data, though through different specific mechanisms.

comparison_rows.dimension: Direct medical and out-of-pocket cost evidence

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports detailed direct medical costs by disease stage, for example a mean of $1,609 per patient in the 1997 cohort for early-stage disease and $4,240 per patient in the 1997 cohort for late-stage disease (2000 dollars), plus extra out-of-pocket drug costs of $164 per patient for early-stage disease in 1997 (2000 dollars).

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper explicitly states it reports no dollar cost data of any kind - no direct medical, non-medical, or out-of-pocket cost figures are given.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Dollar-figure comparisons of burden are only possible when both papers report cost data, and here only the Lyme disease paper does.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper quantifies productivity loss using the human-capital method, finding $411 per patient for early-stage disease versus $7,762 per patient for late-stage disease in the 1997 cohort (2000 dollars).

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports no income loss, lost-workday, or productivity data of any kind.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Work and income loss is a major driver of total burden in the Lyme disease figures but is entirely unmeasured in the Long COVID paper, so this part of the picture is missing for Long COVID.

comparison_rows.dimension: How official data undercounts each condition

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper notes that its own clinical case definition 'may have overestimated' local case counts even as it separately states that CDC national surveillance case counts 'are believed to be underreported,' and it uses the 2002 CDC-reported national count of 23,763 cases to scale its regional cost data.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper finds the standard U09.9 diagnosis code undercounts cases relative to its own algorithm: a PPV-adjusted estimate of about 4,932.52 true-PASC patients among U09.9-coded records, versus about 19,427.48 more patients identified by the algorithm, and the U09.9 approach also skews about 8.7 percentage points more White than the algorithm's cohort.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers show that the method used to define or count cases - not just the underlying disease - strongly shapes how much burden shows up in official data.

comparison_rows.dimension: Subgroup and demographic breakdown of burden figures

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper presents its mean ($1,965) and median ($281) total per-patient cost figures (2000 dollars) as single pooled numbers with no breakdown by age, race/ethnicity, or disability status; sex was tested only for direct medical costs and found no difference.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports its overall PASC prevalence (28.5% raw / 22.77% PPV-adjusted of COVID-19 cases) as a single pooled figure; demographic breakdowns are given only for organ-system-specific symptom odds, not for overall prevalence.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Readers cannot see how either condition's overall burden differs across demographic groups, because both papers pool across subgroups for their headline figures.

comparison_rows.dimension: Overall scope of what kind of burden was measured

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper measures a wide scope of economic burden: direct medical costs, indirect medical costs, nonmedical costs (travel, paid help), and productivity losses, combined into figures such as $8,172 combined direct plus indirect/nonmedical/productivity-loss cost per patient (2000 dollars).

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper's scope is limited to diagnostic and phenotyping accuracy and organ-system symptom prevalence; it explicitly does not measure dollar costs, insurance burden, lost income, or caregiving time.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The two papers measure almost entirely different aspects of burden - one financial, one diagnostic/clinical - so their findings are complementary rather than directly comparable.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper extrapolates its regional per-case costs to a projected nationwide annual economic impact of about $203,000,000 (2002 dollars), based on 23,763 CDC-reported 2002 cases, while flagging this as an uncertain extrapolation given differing case definitions.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper scales its case-identification findings across a large regional health system (over 295,000 patients across 14 hospitals and 20 community health centers in Massachusetts) but does not extrapolate to a national cost or prevalence estimate.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper attempts a nationwide dollar-cost projection; the Long COVID paper's scale-up concerns patient counts and diagnostic methods, not cost.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper collected patient household income via its questionnaire but reports no income-stratified cost analysis or insurance/access-barrier findings in its results.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper explicitly states it reports no insurance coverage, access-barrier, or affordability data.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Neither paper gives the access-to-care evidence a reader would need to understand how affordability barriers affect patients with either condition.

shared_themes.theme: Official counting methods undercount or misrepresent the true number of affected patients, though through different specific mechanisms in each condition.

evidence.note: The paper's clinical case definition may overestimate local case counts, while it separately states CDC national surveillance counts are believed to be underreported, and it scales its cost estimate to that underreported national count.

The standard U09.9 diagnosis code identifies far fewer confirmed long COVID patients than the algorithm (a PPV-adjusted estimate of about 4,932.52 versus about 19,427.48 more patients found by the algorithm) and skews toward White patients by about 8.7 percentage points relative to the algorithm.

shared_themes.theme: Headline burden or prevalence figures are reported as single pooled numbers without breakdown by age, race, disability, or similar subgroups.

evidence.note: The $1,965 mean and $281 median total per-patient cost figures (2000 dollars) are reported pooled across all patients, with no age, race, or disability breakdown.

The overall 28.5% raw / 22.77% PPV-adjusted PASC prevalence figures are reported pooled across all COVID-19 cases, with demographic breakdowns given only for organ-system-specific symptom odds, not overall prevalence.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The paper quantifies a steep rise in cost by disease stage, with late-stage Lyme disease direct medical costs far exceeding early-stage costs.

evidence.note: Mean direct medical cost per patient in the 1997 cohort was $1,609 for early-stage disease versus $4,240 for late-stage disease (2000 dollars), and a regression model found late-stage costs 100% higher than tick-bite-only patients versus 50% higher for early-stage disease (p<0.001).

condition_specific_themes.theme: The paper shows total per-patient costs are heavily right-skewed by a small number of high-cost patients, so the mean cost substantially exceeds the median.

evidence.note: Mean total cost per patient was $1,965 versus a median of $281 (2000 dollars), a gap the paper attributes to a small number of high-cost, mostly late-stage patients.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The paper demonstrates that the diagnostic method chosen (algorithm versus ICD-10 code) substantially changes who counts as a long COVID patient, both in number and demographic composition.

evidence.note: The algorithm identified 24,360 long-haulers with 79.9% precision versus 77.8% precision for the U09.9 code alone, and identified a cohort 8.7 percentage points less White than the U09.9-coded cohort.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The paper documents wide-ranging organ-system symptom burden but contains no economic burden data of any kind.

evidence.note: About 41.2% of long-haulers had systemic symptoms and about 16.4% had gastrointestinal symptoms, but the paper explicitly states it reports no cost, insurance, income-loss, or caregiving-time data.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither the Lyme disease paper nor the Long COVID paper provides insurance coverage, access-barrier, or affordability data, leaving that dimension of burden unmeasured in both of the two papers examined.
Neither paper provides a breakdown of its headline burden or prevalence figures by race, disability status, or similar subgroup categories beyond the limited breakdowns each paper does include.
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers exactly two papers - one real Lyme disease paper (a 2006 CDC-authored regional cost study) and one real Long COVID paper (a 2025 diagnostic-phenotyping study) - and is not a controlled or representative comparison of either condition. The Lyme disease paper offers detailed multi-component dollar cost figures by disease stage, including a mean-versus-median cost skew and a nationwide cost projection, but no demographic breakdown or access-barrier data. The Long COVID paper offers detailed evidence on how diagnostic method changes case counts and demographic composition, but reports no cost, income-loss, or insurance data whatsoever. Where both papers do overlap is in showing that official counting methods undercount or misrepresent true burden, and in pooling their headline figures without subgroup breakdown. Because the two papers measure almost entirely different things, most dimensions in this comparison are one-sided rather than directly comparable, and no conclusions about which condition carries greater overall burden can be drawn from this evidence.
cross_analysis.limitations: This analysis rests on a small, non-random sample: exactly one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, with no papers covering both conditions together, as given in the real_stats (lyme: 1 paper; longCovid: 1 paper; cross: 0 papers; other: 0 papers). This is not a controlled study, the two papers were built from different source documents with different methods, time periods, and price years, and findings here should not be generalized beyond these two specific papers.

learning_cards.headline: Later-stage Lyme costs more, a timing question worth asking
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found that late-stage direct medical costs exceeded early-stage costs by $2631 per patient in the 1997 cohort.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper reports no direct medical costs, so it cannot say whether costs differ depending on how late a patient's case is identified.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers test whether patients identified later, for example through U09.9 coding versus an algorithm, carry higher direct medical costs?

learning_cards.headline: A small high-cost minority can pull average costs upward
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found that mean total cost per patient exceeded the median by $1684, indicating the distribution is right-skewed by a small number of high-cost patients.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper reports no cost data at all, so it cannot say whether its patient counts hide a similar high-cost tail.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Would a cost analysis of the systemic long-haulers identified by the algorithm reveal a similar skew between mean and median costs?

learning_cards.headline: Diagnostic method strongly changes how many patients are counted
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper found that the algorithm-identified count exceeded the PPV-adjusted U09.9 estimate by 19427.48 patients, showing that diagnostic method strongly affects case counts.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper does not compare different diagnostic or surveillance methods, so it cannot say whether its cost figures would shift under a different case-identification approach.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Would Lyme disease cost estimates change if patients were identified using a different diagnostic method than the one used in the 1997 cohort?

learning_cards.headline: Who gets counted can shift with the diagnostic method used
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper found the algorithm-identified cohort had a White-patient share 8.7 percentage points lower than the U09.9-coded cohort.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper reports no demographic breakdown, so it cannot say whether its cost burden differs across patient demographics or identification methods.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Should Lyme disease cost studies check whether demographic composition shifts depending on how patients are identified for inclusion?

learning.takeaway: The Lyme disease paper suggests the Long COVID paper could examine whether cost burdens rise with later case identification or are skewed by a small high-cost minority, while the Long COVID paper suggests the Lyme disease paper could examine whether its patient counts and demographic composition would shift under a different diagnostic method.
